definition: To make two things that seem to conflict fit together or agree with each other.
example: She struggled to reconcile her love of city life with her dream of owning a farm.
nuance: To reconcile is to make conflicting things coexist; to resolve a conflict can simply mean ending it, even if one side loses.
prompt: An accountant finds that the bank statement and the company ledger show different totals.
options: By tracing each deposit, the accountant was able to reconcile the two sets of figures.
The accountant reconciled the totals by pushing them further apart.
The accountant needed a week to reconcile whether she wanted a promotion.
The accountant reconciled the mismatch by shredding the bank statement so no one could compare them.
reasons: Checking each entry until the records match brings the conflicting totals into agreement.
Widening the gap between figures is the opposite of making them agree.
This confuses the word with reconsider; a personal choice is not two records being matched.
Destroying one record hides the conflict instead of making the records consistent.

practice.prompt: A student finds two old travel diaries that give different dates for the same voyage.
options: A calendar change helped the student reconcile the diaries' conflicting dates.
The student reconciled the diaries by copying their dates into a neat spreadsheet.
The student reconciled the two diaries, proving that they could never agree on anything.
The student carefully reconciled the torn pages, gluing them back into the cover.
reasons: Finding a reason the dates differ lets both accounts make sense together.
Organizing the dates neatly does nothing to explain or remove the disagreement.
Showing the accounts are hopelessly at odds is the reverse of bringing them together.
Mending a damaged book is repair, not making conflicting accounts consistent.
